newsitem.title: USA: Toyota U.S. sales rise sharply, Ford up 2.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: Toyota U.S. sales rise sharply, Ford up 2.8 pct.

text.p: Fueled by a weak yen and new models, Toyota Motor Corp. sprinted past Ford Motor Co. on Tuesday with a 55.5 percent increase in January U.S. vehicle sales as its domestic car sales almost doubled.
Toyota's industry-leading sales gain appeared to fulfill analysts' expectations that Japanese automakers are making significant gains in U.S. market share.
Ford, meanwhile, said sales rose 2.8 percent for the month, with a 13.6 percent gain in light truck sales offsetting an 8.1 percent decline in domestic car sales.
General Motors Corp. on Monday reported a 1 percent decline in January sales, while Chrysler Corp. reported a 1.5 percent increase.

"The imports and transplants gained share as expected, at the expense of the Big Three," said Burnham Securities auto analyst David Healy. "They took advantage of the weak yen and offered agressive incentives and lease deals."
Healy said Detroit may have to spend more on incentives, particularly in the mid-size car segment, to try to win customers away from Japanese producers.

The Toyota and Ford results brought the U.S. industry sales for January to a better-than-expected 1.08 million units -- an increase of 6.1 percent over January 1996, with all automakers but Mercedes-Benz AG reporting.
The seasonally adjusted annual sales rate for the month was 15.5 million units, up from 14 million a year ago, when East Coast blizzards kept buyers out of showrooms.

Sales of Toyota and Lexus cars and trucks in January rose to 106,648 cars and trucks from 68,587 in January 1996. Toyota's North American-built car sales, led by an all-new Camry model, rose 90 percent to 54,643 units, while domestic pickup truck sales rose 26.7 percent to 11,157 units.
Toyota's import truck sales, which include its new 4-Runner and RAV4 sport/utility vehicles, jumped 78.4 percent. The RAV4 was just beginning to trickle into dealers in January 1996.
Yale Gieszl, executive vice president of Toyota's U.S. sales arm, Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A Inc., did not mention the yen as a factor in Toyota's gains.

"Continued consumer confidence, combined with a healthy year-end increase in personal income and stable interest rates resulted in a strong month for vehicle sales," he said in a statement. "Overall, the industry is off to a solid start for 1997."

Ford said its truck sales were led by a more than quadrupling of full-size sport/utility vehicles sales to 17,372 units, due to the introduction of the new four-door Expedition, which replaced the two-door Bronco.
But Ford dealers were expected to quickly run short of Expeditions because of a week-old strike at a Johnson Controls Inc. plant that supplies seats for the vehicles. Seat supplies have been halted.

"Demand is so strong that some dealers report they literally can't get one onto the showroom floor," said Ford sales and marketing group Vice President Robert Rewey. "Consumers are lining up to buy them as they're unloaded from the haulaways."

Ford posted mixed car sales results with the Taurus up 9 percent to a record 32,776 units, and the Crown Victoria up 21.3 percent to 10,029 units. Sales of a number of other Ford and Lincoln-Mercury car models fell more than 10 percent.
But the Taurus, America's best-selling car for 1996, was surpassed in January by Toyota's Camry, which registered sales of 36,994 units.
Among other automakers, Germany's Volkswagen AG said it reported its best January sales since 1989. VW said it sold 8,608 vehicles in January, up 19.6 percent over a year ago.
Mazda Motor Corp. sales fell 13.2 percent to 13,385 units, with North American-built car sales down 17.9 percent.
